newsitem.title: JAPAN: NEC says PC shipments up, denies loss of share.
newsitem.headline: NEC says PC shipments up, denies loss of share.

text.p: Japan's biggest personal computer maker NEC Corp said on Wednesday that its first-half domestic PC shipments had surged more than 30 percent and denied reports that it was losing market share.
NEC said the percentage growth in shipments in the half-year to September 30 was against 1.3 million PCs shipped domestically in the same period a year ago.
Yoshi Takayama, NEC's senior vice president, told Reuters that the firm's PC shipments were particularly strong during the summer, after a period of cut-throat price competition subsided.

According to some media reports, NEC has recently suffered a sharp loss in its domestic market share to around 35 percent, due to intensified competition from IBM-compatibles, particularly those made by Fujitsu Ltd.
"Such reports are based on regional surveys and do not reflect the real nationwide trend," Takayama said in an interview.

NEC sells PCs that use its own architecture and although they can run Windows-compatible software, some critics say slight differences in hardware standards can create complications when NEC machines are hooked up to networks with IBM-compatibles.

Takayama said growth in shipments of NEC PCs in the April-September period was more or less in line with the expansion of Japan's total PC market, meaning NEC's market share would not decrease from its current 50 percent.
Private research companies IDC Corp and Dataquest have both estimated NEC's share of the Japanese market last year at about 40 percent.
Takayama also said that NEC would achieve its target of 3.8 million domestic PC shipments in this fiscal year to the end of March 1997, up 28 percent from last year.

He said the planned introduction of IBM-compatible PCs under the Packard Bell-NEC brand -- which some analysts say is a surprising turnaround in NEC's business policy -- would not affect its PC business.
NEC has long said that it will not abandon its own architecture, so as to protect its customers using pre-Windows NEC software.
"With our strong client support system and a wide range of product lines, we'll continue to dominate Japan's PC market with our own-architecture PCs," Takayama said.
The IBM-compatible PCs will be sold by NEC's new joint venture with Packard Bell and Zenith Data Systems of the United States by the end of this year.
